teach.title: A word that describes the doing

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence tells you how the action is done: how the teacher blames, how the soldiers fight?

teach.say: An adjective describes a thing; to describe a doing Latin uses **an adverb (the '-ly' word: how something is done) and its -ius / -issimē forms**. *Iūlia pulchrē cantat* — Julia sings beautifully. It answers 'how?', hangs on the verb rather than on any noun, and never changes its ending.

check.ask: Which word tells you how Marcus writes, rather than what he is like?

teach.title: -us -a -um adjectives take -ē
teach.say: Cut the ending off an adjective of the *-us -a -um* kind and add *-ē*: *rēctus* correct → *rēctē* correctly, *sevērus* strict → *sevērē* sternly, *prāvus* wrong → *prāvē* wrongly, *pulcher* → *pulchrē*. The *-ē* is long, and it stays *-ē* whatever the sentence does.

check.ask: Discipulus bonus semper ____ respondet. Make the adverb of rēctus.

teach.title: Third-declension adjectives take -iter
teach.say: An adjective of the *fortis, -e* kind makes its adverb with *-iter* instead: *fortis* → *fortiter* bravely, *brevis* → *breviter* briefly, *gravis* → *graviter* heavily, *turpis* → *turpiter* shamefully. Take the stem the genitive shows you and put *-iter* on it.

check.ask: Magister ____ respondet, deinde tacet. Make the adverb of brevis.

teach.title: More: the -ius form
teach.say: To say 'more …ly', Latin uses **the comparative (the '-er / more' form)** in its neuter singular, ending *-ius*: *rēctius* more correctly, *fortius* more bravely, *gravius* more heavily. It is the same word as the neuter 'more X thing', doing an adverb's work; with *quam* it sets two doers side by side.

check.ask: Which word here says how Sextus writes, rather than what Sextus is like?

teach.title: Most: the -issimē form
teach.say: To say 'most …ly' or 'very …ly', Latin uses **the superlative (the '-est / most' form)** with *-ē* on the end: *fortissimē* most bravely, *rēctissimē* most correctly. Adjectives in *-er* keep their doubled *r*: *pulcher* → *pulcherrimē*. It is built exactly like the plain adverb in *-ē*, only on the superlative stem.

check.ask: Which word here says how the soldier fights?

teach.title: Adverb or adjective?
teach.say: The two are easy to mix up, because both grow from the same word: **an adjective agreeing with its noun (same gender, number and case)** changes to match that noun, while the adverb never changes at all. In *vōx gravis est, puer graviter respondet* the first word describes the voice and the second the answering.

check.ask: Which of brevis and breviter belongs to the writing rather than to the letter?

core.text: To say *how* something is done, Latin turns an adjective into **an adverb (the '-ly' word: how something is done) and its -ius / -issime forms**. *-us -a -um* adjectives take *-ē*: *rēctus* (correct) → *rēctē* (correctly), *sevērus* (strict) → *sevērē*, *pulcher* → *pulchrē*. 3rd-declension adjectives take *-iter*: *fortis* (brave) → *fortiter*, *brevis* → *breviter*, *turpis* (shameful) → *turpiter*. The comparative adverb is *-ius*, the neuter comparative: *rēctius* — more correctly; the superlative is *-issimē* (*-errimē* for *-er* words): *rēctissimē, pulcherrimē*. An adverb never changes its ending for a noun. Latin name: adverbia.
An adjective describes a thing (*a loud voice*); an adverb describes a doing (*he shouts loudly*). English adds *-ly*; Latin adds *-ē* or *-iter*.

*Sextus rēctus est* and *Sextus rēctē scrībit* — the first describes Sextus, the second his writing. An adjective agreeing with its noun (same gender, number and case) changes with the noun (*puella laeta*, *puerī laetī*); the adverb *laetē* never changes. And do not mistake adverbial *-ē* (long) for the vocative *-e* of *serve!*

more.text: Some adverbs are odd: *bonus* → *bene* (well), *malus* → *male* (badly), *facilis* → *facile* (easily), *multus* → *multum* (much), *magnus* → *magnopere* (greatly); *-ns* adjectives make *-nter*: *prūdēns* → *prūdenter*. Their comparatives are *melius, peius, facilius, plūs, magis*; superlatives *optimē, pessimē, facillimē, plūrimum, maximē*. Neuter accusatives also serve as adverbs: *multum, paulum* (a little), *prīmum* (first).

The learner's notes (week 18): *-us -a -um* and *-er -a -um* adjectives add *-ē* to the stem (the macron distinguishes it from the vocative *-e*): *plēnē, astūtē, pigrē*; 3rd-declension adjectives add *-iter* (*graviter, celeriter*), and after *t* the *-it-* drops to avoid a stutter: *sapienter*; the comparative adverb is *-ius* for every declension (*astūtius, pigrius, celerius*), the superlative *-issimē*, or *-rimē* on the masculine singular of *-er* adjectives (*plēnissimē, pulcherrimē, celerrimē*).

Ørberg (chapter XVIII): adjective *-us -a -um* → adverb *-ē*; adjective *-is -e* → adverb *-iter*; *rēctius, fortius* are comparatives of the adverb, *rēctissimē, fortissimē* superlatives; *nēmō fortius pugnat quam Rōmānī: Rōmānī fortissimē pugnant*. A&G §214–218 give the full set, including *-ō* adverbs (*subitō* suddenly, *falsō* falsely).
One last trap: the adverb ending *-ē* is long, where the short *-e* of *serve!* is the vocative (the form for calling someone).
